label: thm:dirichlet
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:dirichlet}
Let $0<r<R$ and $0<\beta\le2\pi$. For every $E>0$,
\[
 N_{S_{r,R,\beta}}^{\mathrm D}\left(E\right)
 \le\frac{\left|S_{r,R,\beta}\right|}{4\pi}
       \left(E-a_{\mathrm D}\sqrt E\right)_{+}.
\]
For every $k\ge1$, with $W_k=4\pi k/\left|S_{r,R,\beta}\right|$,
\[
 \lambda_k\left(S_{r,R,\beta}\right)
 \ge\left(\sqrt{W_k+a_{\mathrm D}^2/4}+a_{\mathrm D}/2\right)^2
 =W_k+a_{\mathrm D}\sqrt{W_k+a_{\mathrm D}^2/4}
       +a_{\mathrm D}^2/2>W_k.
\]
head: environment
name: Dirichlet correction

label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
Let $0<r<R$ and $0<\beta\le2\pi$. For every $E>0$,
\[
 N_{S_{r,R,\beta}}^{<}\left(E\right)
 >\frac{\left|S_{r,R,\beta}\right|}{4\pi}
       \left(E+a_{\mathrm N}\sqrt E\right).
\]
For every $k\ge1$, with $W_k=4\pi k/\left|S_{r,R,\beta}\right|$,
\[
 \mu_k\left(S_{r,R,\beta}\right)
 <\left(\sqrt{W_k+a_{\mathrm N}^2/4}-a_{\mathrm N}/2\right)^2
 =W_k-a_{\mathrm N}
       \left(\sqrt{W_k+a_{\mathrm N}^2/4}-a_{\mathrm N}/2\right)<W_k.
\]
head: environment
name: Neumann correction

label: prop:continuous
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:continuous}
For every $\delta>0$ and $t>0$,
\[
 M\left(t\right)>\frac D4t^2.
\]
head: environment

label: lem:order-continuity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:order-continuity}
For $v\ge w\ge0$ and every $n\ge0$,
\[
 \frac{v^2-w^2}{R^2}
 \le\lambda_{v,n}-\lambda_{w,n}\le v^2-w^2.
\]
In particular, $n_v\left(t^2\right)$ decreases with $v$, vanishes for
$v>Rt$, and $M$ is continuous on $\left(0,+\infty\right)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

label: prop:angular-transfer
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:angular-transfer}
For normalized radii $1<R$ and $0<\beta\le2\pi$, let
$S=S_{1,R,\beta}$ and $p=\pi/\beta$.
For every $E>0$,
\[
 N_S^{<}\left(E\right)\ge\frac{M\left(\sqrt E\right)}{2p}.
\]
Consequently, Proposition~\ref{prop:continuous} implies
\[
 N_S^{<}\left(E\right)>\frac{\left|S\right|}{4\pi}E,
 \qquad \mu_k\left(S\right)<\frac{4\pi k}{\left|S\right|}\quad(k\ge1).
\]
More generally, any lower bound $M\left(t\right)>Dt^2/4+tB\left(t\right)$
transfers to
\[
 N_S^{<}\left(E\right)>\frac{\left|S\right|}{4\pi}E
              +\frac{\sqrt E}{2p}B\left(\sqrt E\right).
\]
head: environment
name: Angular transfer and the strict energy cutoff

title: Proof
body_md:
{\color{revision}Write $N_S^{\le}\left(E\right)$ for the Neumann count including
eigenvalues equal to $E$. The angular Neumann eigenfunctions are
$\cos\left(jp\theta\right)$, $j\ge0$, each with multiplicity one.
Separation of variables gives}
{\[
 N_S^{\le}\left(t^2\right)=\sum_{j=0}^{+\infty}n_{jp}\left(t^2\right).
\]}
{For $jp\le v\le\left(j+1\right)p$, monotonicity implies
$n_v\left(t^2\right)\le n_{jp}\left(t^2\right)$. Integrating on each
interval and summing gives the left-endpoint comparison}
{\[
 pN_S^{\le}\left(t^2\right)\ge\int_0^{+\infty}n_v\left(t^2\right)\,\mathrm{d} v
 =\frac12M\left(t\right).
\]}
{This comparison alone uses an inclusive energy cutoff. To obtain
strict eigenvalue inequalities, fix $E>0$ and let $E_j\uparrow E$
with $0<E_j<E$. The sector spectrum is discrete, so
$N_S^{\le}\left(E_j\right)\to N_S^{<}\left(E\right)$.
{\color{revision}Passing to the limit using the continuity of $M$ from
Lemma~\ref{lem:order-continuity} gives the first inequality below;
Proposition~\ref{prop:continuous}, proved in Section~\ref{sec:neumann},
gives the strict second inequality:}}
{\[
 pN_S^{<}\left(E\right)
 \ge\frac12M\left(\sqrt E\right)
 >\frac D8 E.
\]}
{Since $D/\left(8p\right)=\left|S\right|/\left(4\pi\right)$, this gives the qualitative
strict counting inequality. Taking $E=4\pi k/\left|S\right|$ gives
$N_S^{<}\left(E\right)>k$: at least $k+1$ eigenvalues, starting with
$\mu_0$, lie strictly below $E$, and hence $\mu_k\left(S\right)<E$.
Conversely, the strict eigenvalue inequalities imply the strict
counting bound by choosing $k=\left\lfloor\left|S\right| E/\left(4\pi\right)\right\rfloor$
when $k\ge1$, and by the constant mode when $k=0$.
{\color{revision}For physical radii $r<rR$, the general remainder transfers as
\[
 N_{S_{r,rR,\beta}}^{<}\left(E\right)
 >\frac{\left|S_{r,rR,\beta}\right|}{4\pi}E
   +\frac{r\sqrt E}{2p}B\left(r\sqrt E\right).
\]
This is the form used in Section~\ref{sec:neumann-quantitative}.}}

label: lem:saw
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Sharp one-sided rounding bounds

label: eq:rounding-phase-change
title: Proof
head: environment

label: lem:all-phase-rounding
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Bounds retaining every initial phase

title: Proof
body_md:
{Keep $g_a$, $Y$, and the nonincreasing weight $w$ from
\eqref{eq:rounding-phase-change}. The lower bound when $a\le1/2$
and the upper bound when $a\ge1/2$ are exactly the initial
half-period estimates in Lemma~\ref{lem:saw}. We verify the two
remaining branches for every terminal phase $Y$.}

{For the upper bound with $0\le a\le1/2$, put $l=1/2-a$.
The initial negative interval $0<y<a$ consists of magnitudes
$l<z<1/2$, with $-z$ occurring at $y=z-l$. The first positive
interval is $a<y<a+1/2=1-l$, with $z$ occurring at
$y=1-l-z$. For $l\le z\le1/2$,}
{\[
 z-l\le1-l-z,\qquad
 z\left[w\left(1-l-z\right)-w\left(z-l\right)\right]\le0.
\]}
{These are precisely the negative and positive values that can be
matched. The residual positive magnitudes are $0<z<l$.
If $Y\le a$, the integral is nonpositive. If
$a<Y\le1-l$, set $r=1-l-Y\in\left[0,1/2\right]$; the included
positive magnitudes are $r<z<1/2$. When $r\ge l$, every included
positive value has a match, and the unmatched negative magnitudes
$l<z<r$ give}
{\[
 I=\int_r^{1/2}z\left[w\left(1-l-z\right)-w\left(z-l\right)\right]\,\mathrm{d} z
   -\int_l^r z\,w\left(z-l\right)\,\mathrm{d} z\le0.
\]}
{When $0\le r<l$, all negative values are matched, and}
{\[
 I=\int_l^{1/2}z\left[w\left(1-l-z\right)-w\left(z-l\right)\right]\,\mathrm{d} z
   +\int_r^l z\,w\left(1-l-z\right)\,\mathrm{d} z
 \le\int_0^l z\,w\left(1-l-z\right)\,\mathrm{d} z.
\]}
{If $Y>1-l$, the same initial decomposition holds with $r=0$,
while the tail starts with a negative half-period and is
nonpositive by~\eqref{eq:rounding-negative-positive} and its
truncated version. Thus in every case,}
{\[
 I\le\int_0^l\frac{z}{\sqrt{2\kappa\left(1-l-z\right)}}\,\mathrm{d} z
 =\frac{C_+\left(a\right)}{\sqrt\kappa}.
\]}
{The endpoint $a=0$ has no initial negative interval and $l=1/2$;
the endpoint $a=1/2$ has no residual positive interval and $l=0$.
The same identities include both endpoints.}

{For the lower bound with $1/2\le a<1$, put $l=a-1/2$.
Match $z$ at $y=l-z$ to $-z$ at $y=l+z$ for $0<z<l$.
The matched integral is nonnegative. A stop with $Y\le l$ is
nonnegative; a stop with $l<Y\le2l$ retains only negative values
that already have a positive match and leaves unmatched positive
values, so it is also nonnegative. For $2l<Y\le a$, formula
\eqref{eq:rounding-initial-positive-pair} with $d=Y-l$ leaves
only the residual negative magnitudes $l<z<d\le1/2$.
For $Y>a$, the same residual interval is complete, and the tail
of positive--negative pairs is nonnegative. It follows that}
{\[
 I\ge-\int_l^{1/2}\frac{z}{\sqrt{2\kappa\left(l+z\right)}}\,\mathrm{d} z
 =-\frac{C_-\left(a\right)}{\sqrt\kappa}.
\]}
{When $a=1/2$ this is the whole initial negative half-period,
since $l=0$. The formulas at $a=1$ agree with those at $a=0$,
as checked below; the initial fractional part itself belongs to
$\left[0,1\right]$ with $1$ excluded.}

{We next evaluate the integral branches. For $0\le a\le1/2$,
write $l=1/2-a$, $B=1/2+a$, $p=\sqrt B$, and $r=\sqrt{2a}$.
The substitution $u=B-z$ gives}
{\begin{align*}
 C_+\left(a\right)
 &=\frac1{\sqrt2}\int_{B-l}^{B}\left(B-u\right)u^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d} u\\
 &=\frac1{\sqrt2}
   \left[2B\sqrt u-\frac23u^{3/2}\right]_{B-l}^{B}\\
 &=\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\left(2p^3-3p^2r+r^3\right)
 =\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\left(p-r\right)^2\left(2p+r\right).
\end{align*}}
{Since $p^2-r^2=l$, replacing $p-r$ by $l/\left(p+r\right)$ proves
\eqref{eq:rounding-Cplus-rationalized}. This replacement also
avoids subtracting nearly equal square roots near $a=1/2$.}

{For $1/2\le a\le1$, write $l=a-1/2$, $p=\sqrt a$, and
$r=\sqrt{2a-1}$. Substitution $u=l+z$ yields}
{\begin{align*}
 C_-\left(a\right)
 &=\frac1{\sqrt2}\int_{2l}^{a}\left(u-l\right)u^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d} u\\
 &=\frac1{\sqrt2}
   \left[\frac23u^{3/2}-2l\sqrt u\right]_{2l}^{a}
 =\frac{\left(3-4a\right)p+r^3}{3\sqrt2}.
\end{align*}}
{The factorization follows by multiplying the numerator by $p+r$:}
{\[
 \left[\left(3-4a\right)p+r^3\right]\left(p+r\right)
 =\left(1-a\right)\left(1+2pr\right),
\]}
{using $p^2=a$ and $r^2=2a-1$. Division by $p+r>0$ proves
\eqref{eq:rounding-Cminus-rationalized}, with no subtractive
cancellation near $a=1$.}

{All branches are nonnegative by their defining integrals or their
explicit positive factors. At the junction and endpoints they give}
{\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &C_+\left(1/2\right)=0,\qquad C_-\left(1/2\right)=1/6,\\
 &C_+\left(0\right)=C_+\left(1\right)=1/3,\qquad C_-\left(0\right)=C_-\left(1\right)=0.
 \end{aligned}
\]}
{The rationalized formulas have positive denominators throughout
their closed intervals, and hence are continuous there; in
particular they also establish continuity at the integrable
singularity of the original $C_+$ integral when $a=0$.
The other branches are continuous directly. Matching values at
$a=1/2$ and at $a=0,1$ therefore give the claimed continuous
periodic extensions.}

{For $C_+$ on $\left[0,1/2\right]$, increasing $a$ shrinks the
positive integration interval and increases the denominator at
every retained $z$, so this branch decreases from $1/3$ to zero.
On $\left[1/2,1\right]$ its power expression increases back to
$1/3$. For $C_-$ on $\left[0,1/2\right]$, the derivative computed
in Lemma~\ref{lem:saw} is positive before $1/4$, vanishes there,
and is negative afterwards; its maximum is $\sqrt2/6$.
On $\left[1/2,1\right]$, increasing $l=a-1/2$ both shrinks the
integration interval $\left[l,1/2\right]$ and enlarges its denominator.
This branch decreases from $1/6$ to zero. Thus}
{\[
 \max_{0\le a\le1} C_+\left(a\right)=\frac13,\qquad
 \max_{0\le a\le1} C_-\left(a\right)=\frac{\sqrt2}{6},
\]}
{as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:rounding-phase-constants}.}

label: cor:Dq-arc-eigen
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:Dq-arc-eigen}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:dirichlet}, whenever
$r\sqrt{W_k}>\mathcal T_\delta$,
\[
\lambda_k-W_k\ge{\frac{4}{r^2D}}
    F_\delta^{\mathrm D}\left(r\sqrt{W_k}\right)>0.
\]
In particular the coefficient of $\sqrt{W_k}$ is
$2\left(R_0+r\right)/\left(R_0^2-r^2\right)$; the displayed errors are
explicit multiples of $W_k^{1/4}$, $W_k^{1/6}$, and one.

name: An explicit gap with the full circular-arc coefficient

title: Proof
body_md:
{At $E=\lambda_k$, right-endpoint sampling gives
$\lambda_k-W_k\ge4B_{\mathrm D}\left(r\sqrt{\lambda_k}\right)/\left(r^2D\right)$.
Use \eqref{eq:Dq-arc-envelope}, the positive threshold, and
$r\sqrt{\lambda_k}\ge r\sqrt{W_k}$.}

label: thm:Dq-certificate-inverse
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: The inverse of the displayed Dirichlet certificates

label: eq:Dq-row-asymptotic
title: Proof
body_md:
{Every $t$ in the set defining \eqref{eq:Dq-sigma} satisfies
$N_S^{\mathrm D}\left(t^2\right)<k$, by
\eqref{eq:Dq-U-upper}.  Since the count includes eigenvalues at
equality, this implies $t<\sqrt{\lambda_k\left(S\right)}$.
Taking the supremum gives the normalized inequality, and scaling
gives \eqref{eq:Dq-sigma-eigen}.}

{The all-index certificate gives}
{\[
 U_{\delta,p}\left(t\right)
 \le{\frac{D}{8p}}\left(t^2-\frac{4c_\delta}D t\right)_{+},\qquad t>0.
\]}
{For $\delta t<\pi$ this follows from $U=0$; otherwise it follows
from $\mathcal B_\delta^{\mathrm D}\left(t\right)\ge c_\delta t$.
The right side is strictly below $k$ for every positive $t$ below}
{\[
 s_k=\sqrt{w_k^2+\frac{4c_\delta^2}{D^2}}+\frac{2c_\delta}D.
\]}
{Hence $\sigma_k\ge s_k$.
Moreover, every sector mode has $n\ge1$ and $jp\ge p\ge1/2$.
The signed comparison gives}
{\[
 \lambda^{\mathrm D}_{jp,n}
 \ge\frac{\pi^2}{\delta^2}+\frac{p^2-1/4}{R^2}.
\]}
{Below the square root of this value the discrete row certificate
itself vanishes.  Consequently $U=0$ there and
$\sigma_k$ is at least that square root.  This proves
\eqref{eq:Dq-sigma-explicit}, including its weaker value
$\pi/\delta$.}

{The normalized sine trial for the transformed radial operator gives
$\lambda^{\mathrm D}_{jp,1}\le\pi^2/\delta^2+j^2p^2-1/4$,
because $\left(j^2p^2-1/4\right)s^{-2}\le j^2p^2-1/4$.
At the energy in \eqref{eq:Dq-sigma-search-endpoint}, the first
$k$ angular ground modes have therefore been counted.  The actual
count, and hence $U_{\delta,p}$, is at least $k$ at every greater
frequency.  This proves the upper search endpoint and also proves
finiteness directly.}

{To prove finiteness and \eqref{eq:Dq-sigma-asymptotic}, first observe
that $p\ge1/2$ eliminates every inner-branch row from the discrete
sum.  Thus \eqref{eq:Dq-discrete-rows} is the lattice count}
{\[
 \mathcal R_{\delta,p}\left(t\right)
 =\#\left\{n,j\ge1:
       \left(\frac{\pi n}\delta\right)^2
       +\left(\frac{pj}R\right)^2
       \le t^2+\frac1{4R^2}\right\}.
\]}
{For fixed $\delta,p$, comparison of each decreasing row with its
integral gives the quadrant-ellipse estimate}
{\begin{equation}\label{eq:Dq-row-asymptotic}
 \mathcal R_{\delta,p}\left(t\right)
 ={\frac{\delta R}{4p}}t^2+O_{\delta,p}\left(t\right).
\end{equation}}
{Indeed, replacing each floor by its argument costs at most one per
row, hence $O_{\delta,p}\left(t\right)$.  Replacing the sum of the
decreasing row lengths by its integral costs another
$O_{\delta,p}\left(t\right)$.  That integral is the quadrant area, and
the added $1/\left(4R^2\right)$ changes it by a bounded quantity.}

{The combined continuous certificate obeys}
{\[
 \mathcal B_\delta^{\mathrm D}\left(t\right)=L_\delta t+o_\delta\left(t\right).
\]}
{Its upper bound is the actual deficit, whose asymptotic is
\eqref{eq:Dq-continuous-asymptotic}{\color{revision}, proved in
Section~\ref{sec:boundary-optimality}}.  Its lower bound is the
included explicit value $F_\delta^{\mathrm D}\left(t\right)
=L_\delta t-O_\delta\left(\sqrt t\right)$ for $t\ge T_\delta$.
It follows that the second entry of \eqref{eq:Dq-U} is}
{\[
{\frac{D}{8p}}t^2-{\frac{L_\delta}{2p}}t+o_{\delta,p}\left(t\right).
\]}
{The leading coefficient in \eqref{eq:Dq-row-asymptotic} is
strictly larger:}
{\[
 {\frac{\delta R}{4p}}-{\frac{D}{8p}}={\frac{\delta^2}{8p}}>0.
\]}
{Therefore the second entry determines the minimum for all
sufficiently large $t$.  In particular $U_{\delta,p}\left(t\right)\to+\infty$,
which proves finiteness of the supremum.  Its positivity follows
already from the zero interval below $\pi/\delta$.}

{Finally, put $a=D/\left(8p\right)$ and $b=L_\delta/\left(2p\right)$.
For every $\eta>0$, and all sufficiently large $t$,}
{\[
 at^2-\left(b+\eta\right)t
 \le U_{\delta,p}\left(t\right)
 \le at^2-\left(b-\eta\right)t.
\]}
{The roots of the two quadratics at height $k$ show, without a
continuity assumption, that}
{\[
 \sigma_k=w_k+\frac b{2a}+o_{\delta,p}\left(1\right).
\]}
{For the upper bound, the first quadratic is increasing above its
large positive root, so every greater $t$ has $U\ge k$.
For the lower bound, values just below the second quadratic's
large positive root have $U<k$.
Squaring and using $b/a=4L_\delta/D$ gives
\eqref{eq:Dq-sigma-asymptotic}.}

label: lem:exact
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:exact}
For every $t>0$ and real $v\ge0$,
\[
 n_v\left(t^2\right)
 =\left\lfloor\frac{\varphi_v\left(Rt\right)-\varphi_v\left(t\right)}{\pi}\right\rfloor+1.
\]
head: environment
name: Real-order phase count

title: Proof
body_md:
{This is \cite[Lemma~2.6]{DaiSunAnnuli} with the integer restriction
removed. The Neumann cross-product vanishes at the integer levels
of $d_v\left(t\right)=\varphi_v\left(Rt\right)-\varphi_v\left(t\right)$.
For real $v>0$, the same phase minimum gives $d_v> -\pi/2$
and $d_v<0$ at small positive $t$; for $v=0$, $d_0$ starts
at zero from above. Normalize the radial solution by
$U\left(1,\lambda\right)=1$, $\partial_sU\left(1,\lambda\right)=0$,
where $\lambda=t^2$. An explicit solution with this normalization is}
{\[
 U\left(s,t^2\right)=\frac{\pi t}{2}
   \left(Y_v'\left(t\right)J_v\left(st\right)
              -J_v'\left(t\right)Y_v\left(st\right)\right).
\]}
{The Bessel Wronskian gives $U\left(1,t^2\right)=1$, and differentiation
in $s$ gives}
{\[
 \partial_sU\left(R,t^2\right)
 =-\frac{\pi t^2}{2}\mathcal M_v\left(t\right)
        \mathcal M_v\left(Rt\right)\sin\left(d_v\left(t\right)\right).
\]}
{At a crossing $d_v\left(t\right)=k\pi$, the same Wronskian yields
$U\left(R,t^2\right)=\left(-1\right)^k\mathcal M_v\left(t\right)/
\left(R\mathcal M_v\left(Rt\right)\right)$.
To check the direction of the crossing, put
$V=\partial_\lambda U$. Differentiating
$\left(sU'\right)'+\left(\lambda s-v^2/s\right)U=0$ gives}
{\[
 \left[s\left(UV'-U'V\right)\right]'=-sU^2.
\]}
{The bracket vanishes at $s=1$. At a Neumann eigenvalue
$U'\left(R\right)=0$, integration and differentiation of the sine
formula above therefore give}
\[
 -R U\left(R,\lambda\right)\,
   \partial_\lambda\partial_sU\left(R,\lambda\right)
 =\int_1^R sU\left(s,\lambda\right)^2\,\mathrm{d} s
 =\frac{\pi t\mathcal M_v\left(t\right)^2}{4}\,d_v'\left(t\right)>0.
\]
{Thus every integer crossing is upward and simple. For $v>0$ the
initial value of $d_v$ lies between $-\pi/2$ and zero, so its first
crossing is at zero; for $v=0$ the zero eigenvalue is already counted
before the first positive crossing at $\pi$. The discrete unbounded
radial spectrum then gives precisely the displayed floor formula.
At an eigenvalue the integer level is included, as required by the
definition of $n_v$. The argument in
\cite[Lemma~2.6]{DaiSunAnnuli} uses these same initial values,
Wronskian, and Lagrange identity; none requires an integer order.}
head: environment

label: lem:analytic-bridge
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:analytic-bridge}
For $5/2\le\delta\le10$ and
$p\left(\delta\right)\le x\le28/5$,
\[
 C_+\left(a_{\mathrm N}\left(x,\delta\right)\right)<\frac{11}{100},
 \qquad
 \mathcal H_{\delta,9/10}\left(x;11/100\right)>\frac{163}{2000}.
\]
head: environment
name: The intermediate-width bridge

title: Proof
body_md:
We use the elementary rational bounds
$333/106<\pi<22/7$ and
\[
 p\left(5/2\right)>\frac{77}{20},\qquad
 p\left(5\right)>\frac{21}{5},\qquad
 p\left(10\right)>\frac{22}{5}.
\]
The three latter inequalities follow by squaring, using
$p\left(5/2\right)^2=1208/81$, $p\left(5\right)^2=872/49$, and
$p\left(10\right)^2=182/9$.

First we control the initial phase throughout the whole bridge.
Set $y=\delta+2$ and
$g\left(\delta\right)=p\left(\delta\right)-3\delta/\left(8p\left(\delta\right)\right)$.
Since
\[
 p^2=24-\frac{48}{y}+\frac{32}{y^2},\qquad
 p'=\frac{8\left(3y-4\right)}{y^3p},\qquad
 p''=-\frac{48\left(y-2\right)}{y^4p}-\frac{\left(p'\right)^2}{p},
\]
we have
\[
 g''
 =p''\left(1+\frac{3\delta}{8p^2}\right)
  +\frac{3p'}{4p^2}-\frac{3\delta\left(p'\right)^2}{4p^3}
 <p''+\frac{3p'}{4p^2}<0.
\]
{For clarity, differentiating once first gives}
{\[
 g'=p'\left(1+\frac{3\delta}{8p^2}\right)-\frac3{8p},
\]}
{and differentiating again gives the displayed expression for
$g''$. The extra terms containing $\delta$ are negative because
$p''<0$, $p'>0$, and $\delta>0$.
Indeed, on $9/2\le y\le12$,}
\[
 \frac{y\left(3y-4\right)}{8\left(y-2\right)}
 =\frac{3y+2+4/\left(y-2\right)}8
 \le\frac{99}{20}<9<p^2,
\]
{which makes the last upper bound strictly negative.
Indeed,}
{\[
 p''+\frac{3p'}{4p^2}
 <-\frac{48\left(y-2\right)}{y^4p}
       +\frac{6\left(3y-4\right)}{y^3p^3}<0
\]}
{is precisely the comparison
$p^2>y\left(3y-4\right)/\left(8\left(y-2\right)\right)$ proved above.
The concavity of $g$ therefore reduces its lower bound to its two
endpoints. The function $z-3\delta/\left(8z\right)$ increases with $z>0$;
hence}
\[
 \frac{g\left(5/2\right)}\pi
 >\frac{19439}{16940}>\frac{111}{100},\qquad
 \frac{g\left(10\right)}\pi
 >\frac{10927}{9680}>\frac{111}{100}.
\]
The unwrapped initial phase increases with $x$. Its upper bound is
attained at $x=28/5$ and $\delta=5/2$, so
\[
 \frac{x-3\delta/\left(8x\right)}\pi
 \le\frac{12169}{2240\pi}
 <\frac{12169\cdot106}{2240\cdot333}<\frac{173}{100}.
\]
Consequently its fractional part stays in $\left(11/100,73/100\right)$.
The half-period monotonicity of $C_+$ reduces its bound to these
two endpoints. Its explicit formulas give
\[
 C_+\left(11/100\right)
 <\frac12\left(\frac{39}{100}\right)^2
       \frac{21/10}{\left(121/100\right)^2}
 =\frac{31941}{292820}<\frac{11}{100},
\]
where we used
$\sqrt2<3/2$, $3/4<\sqrt{61/100}<4/5$, and
$23/50<\sqrt{22/100}<1/2$. Also,
\[
 C_+\left(73/100\right)
 =\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}\left(\frac{23}{100}\right)^{3/2}
 <\frac{20}{21}\frac{23}{100}\frac{12}{25}
 =\frac{92}{875}<\frac{11}{100}.
\]

It remains to show positivity of the envelope. Denote its core and
outer rounding errors by $r=\left(11/50\right)/\sqrt{K_\delta\left(p\right)}$
and $s$. The arithmetic--geometric mean inequality implies
\[
 K_\delta\left(p\right)
 \ge2\sqrt{\frac{23\delta}{24\pi^2\left(1+\delta\right)}}
 >2\sqrt{\frac{5635}{81312}}>\frac{13}{25},
 \qquad r<\frac{31}{100}.
\]
{Here $\delta/\left(1+\delta\right)\ge5/7$ and $\pi<22/7$
give the middle lower bound. The last two comparisons reduce to}
{\[
 \frac{4\cdot5635}{81312}>\left(\frac{13}{25}\right)^2,
 \qquad
 \frac{\left(11/50\right)^2}{13/25}
 =\frac{121}{1300}<\left(\frac{31}{100}\right)^2.
\]}
Since $\sqrt{\delta\left(\delta+2\right)}<\delta+1$,
\[
 s<\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{9p}}\left(\delta+\frac12\right).
\]
{\color{editorial}Using $I\left(9/10\right)<111/500$ from
Lemma~\ref{lem:endpoint-estimates}, on $5/2\le\delta\le5$ we obtain}
\[
 s<\frac{427}{1000}\left(\delta+\frac12\right),\qquad
 \frac{2\delta I\left(9/10\right)}p<\frac{116}{1000}\delta,
\]
and hence
\[
 \mathcal H_{\delta,9/10}\left(p;11/100\right)
 >\frac{593}{2000}-\frac{43}{1000}\delta
 \ge\frac{163}{2000}.
\]
On $5\le\delta\le10$, the sharper lower bound $p>21/5$ gives
\[
 s<\frac{408}{1000}\left(\delta+\frac12\right),\qquad
 \frac{2\delta I\left(9/10\right)}p<\frac{106}{1000}\delta,
\]
and therefore
\[
 \mathcal H_{\delta,9/10}\left(p;11/100\right)
 >\frac{153}{500}-\frac7{500}\delta
 \ge\frac{83}{500}>\frac{163}{2000}.
\]
Each constant comparison just used is a comparison of positive
rational numbers after squaring; for example the two outer
coefficients follow from
$880/4851<\left(427/1000\right)^2$ and
$220/1323<\left(408/1000\right)^2$.
Frequency monotonicity of the envelope extends these lower bounds
from $x=p\left(\delta\right)$ to the full bridge. Its proof applies already
at $\delta=5/2$, because
$\delta\sqrt{\delta\left(\delta+2\right)}/\left(1+\delta\right)>2$
there and this expression increases with $\delta$.

label: lem:Nq-cutoff-opt
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Nq-cutoff-opt}
For every $t>0$ the minimum in \eqref{eq:Nq-cutoff-loss} is
attained at a unique cutoff $u_*\left(t\right)$.  The minimizing cutoff is $u_*\left(t\right)=0$ for
$0<t\le t_c$.  For $t>t_c$, $u_*\left(t\right)$ is the unique root in $\left(0,1\right)$ of
\[
\frac{9-2u^2}{12\pi\left(1-u^2\right)^{3/2}}
       =t\left(1+2c\left(ut\right)\right).
\]
Both $u_*$ and $j$ are continuous.

title: Proof

label: prop:Nq-count
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
{On the core $\left[0,ut\right]$ use exactly the phase and directional
rounding estimates proved above.  On the turning interval use
$n_v\left(t^2\right)>f_t\left(v\right)-c\left(v\right)$ pointwise.  Its positive length gives
strictness after integration.  The reflected outer rounding
estimate is unchanged.  The result is}
{\[
 M\left(t\right)>\frac D4t^2+bt
  -\frac{2C_+\left(a\left(t\right)\right)}{\sqrt{\kappa_{\rm in}}}
  -\frac{\sqrt2}{3\sqrt{\kappa_{\rm out}}}-J\left(t,u\right),
\]}
{where $t^2\kappa_{\rm in}=K_\delta\left(\delta t\right)$ and
$t^{-1}/\sqrt{\kappa_{\rm out}}=
\sqrt{\pi\sqrt D/t}$.  At $u=0$ the same estimate holds by
continuity, and dropping the absent core gives the sharper
bound $B_0$.  Evaluate the positive-core bound at the attained
optimizer, and combine it with \eqref{eq:Nq-trial-opt}.}

{We spell out why the envelope is quantitatively positive at
every junction of the earlier cover.  For $0<\delta\le5/2$,
the constant trial gives a positive remainder on
$0<x\le15/4$, the phase window has margin $453/2000$ on
$15/4\le x\le27/5$, and the thin tail has margin $1/250$
above $27/5$.  Our integrated cap is at least as good as the
cap $1/4$ there, because $v\ge\left(9/10\right)t\ge27/20$ on the
turning interval.  For $5/2\le\delta\le10$, the power trial
has positive remainder up to and including $x=p\left(\delta\right)$
because $\widehat V_R\left(t\right)>v_*\left(t\right)$.  The intermediate bridge
has margin $163/2000$, and the larger-width tail has margin
$7/400$.  For $\delta\ge10$, the power interval overlaps the
generic $u=3/4$ range with margin $1/20$.  Each old $G$ or
$\mathcal H$ estimate is bounded above by
\eqref{eq:Nq-Bphase}, since the integrated cap is smaller and
the cutoff has been optimized.  These intervals cover every
positive $\delta,t$, proving positivity.}

{Continuity of the trial maximum follows from its continuous
formula on a compact interval, or by reparametrizing
$\alpha=zRt$, $0\le z\le1$.  Continuity of the other terms
has already been established.  Finally $V_R\left(t\right)\le Rt$, so
$B_{\rm tr}\left(t\right)\to-\infty$.  The core and outer rounding
losses in $B_{\rm ph}$ tend to zero.  Choosing
$1-u=t^{-2/3}$ for $t>1$ shows $j\left(t\right)=O\left(t^{1/3}\right)$.
Hence $B_{\rm ph}\left(t\right)\to b$; all its losses are nonnegative,
and $B_0\left(t\right)\le b$, proving the asserted limit.}

title: Proof

label: prop:Nq-actual-coefficient
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Nq-actual-coefficient}
\label{prop:Dq-continuous-asymptotic}
For each fixed $R>1$,
\[
M_{\mathrm N}\left(t\right)=\frac D4t^2+\frac{R+1}2t+o_R\left(t\right),
 \qquad t\longrightarrow+\infty,
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Dq-continuous-asymptotic}
 M_{\mathrm D}\left(t\right)=\frac D4t^2-\frac{R+1}2t+o_R\left(t\right).
\end{equation}
Hence $\left(R+1\right)/2$ is the largest possible leading coefficient in a
lower bound, with an $o_R\left(t\right)$ remainder, for either the actual
Neumann surplus $M_{\mathrm N}\left(t\right)-Dt^2/4$ or the actual Dirichlet
deficit $Dt^2/4-M_{\mathrm D}\left(t\right)$.
head: environment
name: The sharp continuous boundary coefficient

title: Proof
body_md:
{On a compact interval $I$ contained in $\left(0,1\right)$ or $\left(1,R\right)$, the
change of variable $y=g_R\left(z\right)$ gives a smooth bounded weight with
bounded derivative.  If $H$ is a bounded Riemann integrable function
of period one and mean zero, its bounded periodic primitive and
integration by parts give}
{\[
 \int_I H\left(tg_R\left(z\right)+c\right)\,\,\mathrm{d} z=O_I\left(t^{-1}\right).
\]}
{The same conclusion applies to the sawtooth, and to an indicator
of a fixed interval modulo one after subtracting its mean.
In particular,}
{\[
 \int_I\left(\left\lfloor tg_R\left(z\right)+c\right\rfloor-tg_R\left(z\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d} z
       \longrightarrow\left(c-1/2\right)\left|I\right|.
\]}
{The uniform convergence of $r_t^\sigma$ to the constant $c$ in
\eqref{eq:Bq-phase-shifts} preserves this limit.  For a phase
perturbation of size at most $\eta<1/2$, the floor can change
only within distance $\eta$ of an integer.  The change of variable
just used bounds the measure of this set by $O_I\left(\eta+t^{-1}\right)$.
Let $t\to+\infty$ and then $\eta\downarrow0$.}

{The mean corrections $n_{tz}^\sigma\left(t^2\right)-f_t\left(tz\right)$ are therefore
$1/2$ and $1/4$ for Neumann conditions on the inner and outer order
regions, and $-1/2$ and $-1/4$ for Dirichlet conditions.  The
uniform bounds \eqref{eq:Bq-uniform-N}--\eqref{eq:Bq-uniform-D}
allow intervals about $z=0,1,R$ to be removed and then shrunk.
It follows that}
{\[
 \int_0^R\left(n_{tz}^{\mathrm N}\left(t^2\right)-f_t\left(tz\right)\right)\,\mathrm{d} z
       \longrightarrow\frac12+\frac\delta4=\frac{R+1}4,
\]}
{and the Dirichlet limit is its negative.  Multiplication by $2t$
and the exact action identity \eqref{eq:action} prove both formulas.
The final assertion follows by dividing the corresponding surplus
or deficit by $t$.}
head: environment

label: lem:Bq-discrete-averaging
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Discrete averaging of the action

title: Proof
body_md:
{Set $F_t\left(x\right)=h t g_R\left(px/t\right)$ on the real interval $\left(t/p\right)I$.
By \eqref{eq:Bq-action-curvature}, $F_t'$ is monotone with a
range contained in a fixed bounded interval, and}
{\[
 \frac{a}{t}\le\left|F_t''\left(x\right)\right|\le\frac{b}{t}
\]}
{for positive constants $a,b$ depending only on the fixed data.
For $0<\varepsilon<1/4$, remove the set}
{\[
 \left\{x:\operatorname{dist}\left(F_t'\left(x\right),\mathbb Z\right)<\varepsilon\right\}.
\]}
{There are only a fixed number of its component intervals, and
their total length is $O\left(\varepsilon t\right)$, by the lower derivative
bound.  Discard every integer index $j$ whose edge $\left[j,j+1\right]$
meets that set, together with the endpoint indices whose edges
are not wholly contained in $\left(t/p\right)I$.  This discards
$O\left(\varepsilon t+1\right)$ terms.}

{The retained indices form a fixed number of consecutive blocks.
On each block the differences
$d_j=F_t\left(j+1\right)-F_t\left(j\right)$ are monotone and belong to a single interval
$\left[m+\varepsilon,m+1-\varepsilon\right]$ for an integer $m$.
Put}
{\[
 u_j=e^{2\pi\mathrm iF_t\left(j\right)},\qquad
 a_j=\frac1{e^{2\pi\mathrm i d_j}-1}
       =-\frac12-\frac{\mathrm i}2\cot\left(\pi d_j\right).
\]}
{Then $u_j=a_j\left(u_{j+1}-u_j\right)$.  Summation by parts on a block
$A\le j\le B$ gives}
{\[
 \sum_{j=A}^B u_j
 =a_Bu_{B+1}-a_Au_A+
       \sum_{j=A+1}^B\left(a_{j-1}-a_j\right)u_j.
\]}
{The cotangent is monotone between successive integers.  Hence
$\sup\left|a_j\right|+\sum\left|a_{j-1}-a_j\right|=O\left(\varepsilon^{-1}\right)$ on the
block.  Restoring the discarded terms proves}
{\[
 \left|\sum_{pj/t\in I}e^{2\pi\mathrm i h f_t\left(pj\right)}\right|
       =O\left(\varepsilon t+\varepsilon^{-1}+1\right).
\]}
{Choose $\varepsilon=t^{-1/2}$ for sufficiently large $t$ to obtain
\eqref{eq:Bq-exponential-sum}.}

{The number of indices is $t\left|I\right|/p+O\left(1\right)$.  The exponential-sum
estimate first proves \eqref{eq:Bq-discrete-mean} for trigonometric
polynomials.  Uniform approximation by the Fej\'er polynomials
proves it for continuous
periodic functions.  Continuous majorants and minorants for
interval indicators then give it for step functions; upper and
lower step approximations give the stated Riemann integrable case.
This also supplies a direct proof of the asserted equidistribution.}
head: environment

label: thm:Bq-full-perimeter
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:Bq-full-perimeter}
Let $S=S_{r,R_{\rm phys},\beta}$, with $0<r<R_{\rm phys}$ and
$0<\beta\le2\pi$, retaining the slit at the endpoint.  Put
\[
 A=\left|S\right|=\frac\beta2\left(R_{\rm phys}^2-r^2\right),\qquad
 P=\beta\left(R_{\rm phys}+r\right)+2\left(R_{\rm phys}-r\right).
\]
For either the strict or the inclusive counting convention,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Bq-full-perimeter}
 \begin{aligned}
 N_S^{\mathrm N,<}\left(E\right),\ N_S^{\mathrm N,\le}\left(E\right)
       &=\frac A{4\pi}E+\frac P{4\pi}\sqrt E+o_S\left(\sqrt E\right),\\
 N_S^{\mathrm D,<}\left(E\right),\ N_S^{\mathrm D,\le}\left(E\right)
       &=\frac A{4\pi}E-\frac P{4\pi}\sqrt E+o_S\left(\sqrt E\right),
 \qquad E\longrightarrow+\infty.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: Two-term law for a fixed annular sector

title: Proof
body_md:
{For normalized radii, separation of variables gives the inclusive
Neumann sum over $j\ge0$ and the Dirichlet sum over $j\ge1$.
Combining \eqref{eq:Bq-sampled-corrections} and
\eqref{eq:Bq-action-sums} gives}
{\[
 N_S^{\sigma,\le}\left(t^2\right)=\frac D{8p}t^2
       \mathbin{\pm}\left(\frac{R+1}{4p}
                     +\frac\delta{2\pi}\right)t+o_{R,p}\left(t\right),
\]}
{with the plus sign for Neumann and the minus sign for Dirichlet.}

{For a fixed angular order every radial eigenvalue is simple.
Thus the strict and inclusive radial counts differ by at most one,
and a difference requires $\gamma_t^\sigma\left(jp\right)$ to be an integer.
On each compact order interval, local uniformity of the phase
shift forces $f_t\left(jp\right)+c$ into a shrinking neighborhood of the
integers.  Lemma~\ref{lem:Bq-discrete-averaging} shows that there
are $o\left(t\right)$ such indices.  The endpoint intervals contribute at
most $O\left(\eta t+1\right)$ further coincidences.  Shrinking them proves
that the total difference between the two sector conventions is
$o\left(t\right)$.}

{Finally take $R=R_{\rm phys}/r$ and $t=r\sqrt E$.
The quadratic coefficient becomes $A/\left(4\pi\right)$, the coefficient
$\left(R+1\right)/\left(4p\right)$ becomes the circular-arc term
$\beta\left(R_{\rm phys}+r\right)/\left(4\pi\right)$, and $\delta/\left(2\pi\right)$ becomes
the term $2\left(R_{\rm phys}-r\right)/\left(4\pi\right)$ for the two radial sides.
This proves \eqref{eq:Bq-full-perimeter}, including the retained
slit, whose two faces both belong to the boundary.}
head: environment

label: cor:product
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:product}
Let $S=S_{r,R,\beta}$ satisfy the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, be a
bounded connected Lipschitz domain. With Neumann conditions on
the whole product boundary,
\[
 \mu_k\left(S\times\Omega\right)
 <4\pi^2\left(\frac{k}{\omega_{d+2}\left|S\right|\left|\Omega\right|}\right)^{2/\left(d+2\right)},
 \qquad k\ge1.
\]
At $\beta=2\pi$ the slit is retained in the product form.

label: lem:endpoint-estimates
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:endpoint-estimates}
Set
\[
 d=\frac52,\qquad x_0=\frac{15}{4},\qquad
 X_0=\frac{27}{5},\qquad x_B=\frac{22}{5},
\]
and write the three frequency-dependent errors as
\[
 r_\delta\left(x;c\right)=\frac{2c}{\sqrt{K_\delta\left(x\right)}},\qquad
 s_\delta\left(x\right)=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{9x}}
              \delta^{3/4}\left(\delta+2\right)^{1/4},\qquad
 \ell_{\delta,u}\left(x\right)=\frac{2\delta I\left(u\right)}{x}.
\]
Then
\[
 \frac{333}{106}<\pi<\frac{355}{113}<\frac{22}{7},\qquad
 \frac{11}{50}<I\left(9/10\right)<\frac{111}{500},\qquad
 I\left(3/4\right)<\frac{129}{1000}.
\]
The low-frequency endpoint satisfies
\[
 a_d>\frac{211}{100},\qquad
 2a_dx_0-\frac{2+d}{4}x_0^2>\frac3{640}.
\]
On the thin-width phase window its fractional initial phase lies
between $1/9$ and $18/25$, and
\[
 C_+\left(1/9\right)<\frac1{10},\qquad
 C_+\left(18/25\right)<\frac1{10},\qquad
 c\left(27/20\right)<\frac14.
\]
The window constants obey
\[
 r_d\left(x_0;1/10\right)<\frac7{25},\qquad
 \sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{9x_0}}<\frac{54}{125}.
\]
At $\left(\delta,x\right)=\left(d,X_0\right)$, the generic
tail errors and their width derivatives satisfy
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 r_d\left(X_0;1/3\right)&<\frac{21}{25},&
 s_d\left(X_0\right)&<\frac{21}{20},&
 \ell_{d,9/10}\left(X_0\right)&<\frac{103}{500},\\
 \partial_\delta r_d\left(X_0;1/3\right)&>\frac{11}{200},&
 \partial_\delta s_d\left(X_0\right)&>\frac{73}{200},&
 \partial_\delta\ell_{d,9/10}\left(X_0\right)&>\frac{11}{135}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here and below $\partial_\delta r_d$ means the derivative evaluated
at $\delta=d$; the frequency and the coefficient are held fixed.
For the wide-width argument,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 r_{10}\left(x_B;1/3\right)&<\frac{737}{1000},&
 s_{10}\left(x_B\right)&<\frac{417}{100},&
 \ell_{10,3/4}\left(x_B\right)&<\frac{587}{1000},\\
 \partial_\delta s_{10}\left(x_B\right)&<\frac25,&
 \partial_\delta\ell_{10,3/4}\left(x_B\right)&<\frac3{50},&
 p\left(10\right)&>x_B.
 \end{aligned}
\]
head: environment
name: \textcolor{revision}{Constants for the frequency and width cover

title: Proof
body_md:
{For $0<z<1$, the alternating expansion}
{\[
 \arctan z=z-\frac{z^3}{3}+\frac{z^5}{5}-\cdots
\]}
{places $\arctan z$ between consecutive truncations. Machin's identity
$\pi=16\arctan\left(1/5\right)-4\arctan\left(1/239\right)$ follows from
$\tan\left(4\arctan\left(1/5\right)\right)=120/119$ and the tangent
subtraction formula, which gives
$\tan\left(4\arctan\left(1/5\right)-\arctan\left(1/239\right)\right)=1$.
The angle is in $\left(0,\pi/2\right)$, so it equals $\pi/4$.
The truncation bounds now give}
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \pi&>
 16\left(\frac15-\frac1{3\cdot5^3}
       +\frac1{5\cdot5^5}-\frac1{7\cdot5^7}\right)-\frac4{239}
 >\frac{333}{106},\\
 \pi&<
 16\left(\frac15-\frac1{3\cdot5^3}
       +\frac1{5\cdot5^5}-\frac1{7\cdot5^7}
       +\frac1{9\cdot5^9}\right)
 -4\left(\frac1{239}-\frac1{3\cdot239^3}\right)
 <\frac{355}{113}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
{The first display uses a four-term lower bound for $\arctan\left(1/5\right)$
and the one-term upper bound for $\arctan\left(1/239\right)$;
the second uses a five-term upper bound and a two-term lower bound.
Thus the inequality directions account for both signs in Machin's identity.}

For $w=\sqrt{19}$, we have $87/20<w<109/25$ and
\[
 I\left(9/10\right)
 =\frac1{24}+\frac{63/w-2\arctan\left(w/9\right)}{24\pi}.
\]
The inequalities $z-z^3/3<\arctan z<z$ for $0<z<1$ give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \frac{63}{w}-2\arctan\left(w/9\right)
 &>\frac{1575}{109}-\frac{218}{225}
   >\frac{107}{25}\frac{22}{7},\\
 \frac{63}{w}-2\arctan\left(w/9\right)
 &<\frac{420}{29}-\frac{29}{30}
      +\frac23\left(\frac{109}{225}\right)^3
   <\frac{541}{125}\frac{333}{106}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
They prove the asserted two-sided bound for $I\left(9/10\right)$.
For $w=\sqrt7>66/25$, put $z=\left(3-w\right)/\left(3+w\right)<3/47$.
Since $\arctan\left(w/3\right)=\pi/4-\arctan z$,
\[
 I\left(3/4\right)
 =\frac1{48}+\frac{21/w+2\arctan z}{24\pi}
 <\frac1{48}+\frac{175/22+6/47}{24\left(333/106\right)}
 <\frac{129}{1000}.
\]

For the logarithm, the positive power series for
$\log\left(\left(1+z\right)/\left(1-z\right)\right)$ at $z=5/9$ gives
\[
 \log\left(7/2\right)
 <2\left(\frac59+\frac13\left(\frac59\right)^3\right)
   +\frac{2\left(5/9\right)^5}{5\left(1-\left(5/9\right)^2\right)}
 =\frac{76915}{61236}<\frac{63}{50}.
\]
{The tail estimate above follows by replacing the denominators
$5,7,9,\ldots$ by $5$ in the remaining positive terms and summing
the resulting geometric series. Since $D=d\left(d+2\right)=45/4$,}
{\[
 a_d^2=\frac{45/4}{2\log\left(7/2\right)}
 >\frac{45/4}{2\left(63/50\right)}=\frac{125}{28}
 >\left(\frac{211}{100}\right)^2.
\]}
{Substitution of $x_0=15/4$ then gives}
{\[
 2a_dx_0-\frac{2+d}{4}x_0^2
 >2\frac{211}{100}\frac{15}{4}
    -\frac98\left(\frac{15}{4}\right)^2=\frac3{640}.
\]}

{The endpoint bounds for the shifted initial phase on the thin-width window are}
\[
 \frac7{2\pi}-1>\frac5{44}>\frac19,
 \qquad
 \frac{27}{5\pi}-1<\frac{113}{157}<\frac{18}{25}.
\]
{The unwrapped initial phase $x/\pi-3\delta/\left(8\pi x\right)$
increases with $x$ and decreases with $\delta$. Its extrema on
$x_0\le x\le X_0$, $0<\delta\le d$ are therefore bounded
by the two displayed endpoints. For the left phase, use}
{\[
 C_+\left(a\right)=\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\left(\frac12-a\right)^2
 \frac{2\sqrt{1/2+a}+\sqrt{2a}}
       {\left(\sqrt{1/2+a}+\sqrt{2a}\right)^2},
 \qquad 0\le a\le\frac12,
\]}
{together with}
\[
 \frac{39}{50}<\sqrt{\frac{11}{18}}<\frac{79}{100},\qquad
 \frac{47}{100}<\sqrt{\frac29}<\frac{12}{25},\qquad
 \sqrt2<\frac{177}{125}.
\]
It follows that
\[
 C_+\left(1/9\right)
 <\frac{59}{125}\frac{49}{324}\frac{103}{50}\frac{16}{25}
 =\frac{595546}{6328125}<\frac1{10}.
\]
For the right phase,
\[
 C_+\left(18/25\right)^2
 =\frac89\left(\frac{11}{50}\right)^3<\frac1{100}.
\]
The half-period monotonicity of $C_+$ now controls every phase
in the window.

For the turning cap, let $w=\sqrt{871}$, so
$59/2<w<148/5$, and define
\[
 z=\frac{w-27}{w+27}>\frac5{113}.
\]
Then
\[
